opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting puzzle, and I should say up front that I don't think anybody has a fully worked-out answer yet. But here's how I think about it.

The classic picture of perception, the predictive processing picture, says that what you experience isn't just the raw input coming up from your eyes. It's a combination of that bottom-up signal with a lot of top-down expectation, your brain's guesses about what's out there. And one natural thought is that mental imagery is the top-down system running on its own, without much input from the world. When you picture your grandmother's kitchen, you're using the same generative machinery that ordinarily helps you see, but you're running it offline.

So if you take that picture seriously, you might expect that people with aphantasia, people who report no visual imagery at all, would have some kind of deficit in top-down processing more generally. Maybe they'd be worse at perceiving ambiguous figures, or less susceptible to certain illusions, or worse at visual memory.

What's striking is that, for the most part, that's not what you find. People with aphantasia often do perfectly well on many tasks that seem to require imagery. They can answer questions like "Which is darker green, a pea or a pine tree?" They can do mental rotation tasks, sometimes a bit differently or more slowly, but they get there. Many of them are perfectly successful scientists and artists, and they don't even realize they're different until someone asks them about it.

So I'd put it this way. It's not that the top-down system is broken. It's more that there's a dissociation between having the information, the generative model that lets you make predictions and answer questions, and having the conscious, quasi-perceptual experience of that information. The model is there and working. What's missing is the bit where it gets rendered, as it were, into something that feels like seeing.

And that's interesting for a developmental psychologist, because it reminds us how little our introspective reports tell us about what's actually going on computationally. We assume everybody's inner life is like ours. Francis Galton found back in the nineteenth century that some of his scientific colleagues insisted mental imagery was just a figure of speech. And those of us who have vivid imagery assume that's what thinking is like. It turns out there's enormous variation in conscious experience that doesn't map neatly onto differences in what people can actually do.

There's also some evidence that aphantasics show differences in things like sensory responses to frightening stories, or in how much prior imagery primes later perception. So there may be a narrower, more specific link between imagery and perception that's absent. But "broken top-down processing" is too strong. It's more like there are many different kinds of top-down influence, and imagery is just one particular, quite optional, way of experiencing them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mental imagery and generative machinery but does not say that generating a visual representation activates the visual cortex as a contingent side effect.

r002.rationale: It describes a dissociation between aphantasia and the underlying generative model, which remains working, and reports that people with aphantasia can succeed at tasks that seem to require imagery.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think aphantasia is actually a really interesting case, because it's one of the places where you can see that the picture of the mind as just a machine for generating predictions, where everything is this very top-down, constructive process, doesn't quite capture the whole story.

So the standard view in a lot of cognitive science now, the predictive-processing view, is that what you're doing when you perceive something is you're generating a model from the top down, and then the data from the world comes in and corrects that model. And mental imagery, on that view, is sort of what you get when you run the top-down part without the bottom-up part. You generate the model, but there's nothing coming in to constrain it.

What's striking about aphantasia is that people who report having no mental imagery at all seem to function perfectly well in all sorts of ways that you would think would depend on that top-down machinery. They can recognize faces, they can navigate, they can remember what their kitchen looks like in the sense of being able to answer questions about it. They just don't have the phenomenology, the sense of a picture in the mind's eye. So I don't think it's right to say that the top-down processing is broken. What seems to be different is something more like the access to that processing, or the way it gets represented consciously.

And actually, I think this connects to something I've been interested in for a long time, which is the difference between the kind of knowledge that's explicit and accessible to you and the kind that's doing a lot of work under the hood. Young children, for instance, have these very rich causal models of the world that they clearly use, but they can't tell you about them. And I suspect that imagery, in the vivid sense, might be more like a particular style of conscious access to those models, one that some people have a lot of and some people have very little of, rather than being the models themselves.

The other thing I'd say is that we should be a bit skeptical of self-report here. One of the things we know from the history of introspection in psychology is that people are not very good at reporting on their own mental processes. So some of what's going on with aphantasia may be differences in how people interpret the question, "Do you see a picture?" But I don't think that's all of it, because there are now some fairly nice behavioral and physiological studies, things like pupil responses to imagined bright objects, where the aphantasic people genuinely look different. So something real is going on. I just don't think it's that the generative machinery is missing. It's more that the window onto it is different.

r001.rationale: The response discusses top-down models, imagery, and differences in conscious access, but does not state that generating a mental visual representation activates the visual cortex as a contingent side effect.

r002.rationale: It says aphantasic people can recognize faces, navigate, and answer questions about familiar scenes, and argues that the generative machinery is not missing; this conveys that visual-representation capacity can remain intact despite absent imagery phenomenology.

astra-6.text:
I think “broken” is probably too strong. Top-down processing covers a lot of different things. One is that what you already know influences what you perceive. Another is that you can generate an experience in the absence of the thing itself—you can close your eyes and picture an apple. Those needn’t be exactly the same capacity.

What’s interesting about aphantasia is that people report not having that second kind of experience, yet they can recognize things, reason about them, and navigate the world. So it suggests that having a conscious visual image isn’t necessary for all the things we might have thought depended on it. You could still have expectations shaping your perception without being able to summon up a picture voluntarily.

But I don’t think we yet know precisely where that difference lies. Is it in generating the representation, or in the representation becoming consciously available? Part of what makes this so fascinating is how little access we have to differences in other people’s experience. We say, “Imagine an apple,” and assume that everybody is doing the same thing. Apparently, they aren’t.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes voluntary imagery from other top-down effects, but does not mention visual cortex activation or describe it as a side effect.

r002.rationale: It raises whether the difference lies in generating a representation or making it consciously available, but does not state that aphantasia can leave visual-representation generation intact.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure that “broken” is the right way to think about it. Top-down processing does lots of things besides giving us conscious visual images. Your expectations can shape what you perceive without your being able to conjure up a picture with your eyes closed.

So one possibility is that aphantasia reflects a difference in how those processes become available to consciousness, rather than an absence of top-down processing altogether. You might still have representations that let you recognize things, reason about space, and make predictions, without experiencing them as pictures.

What’s fascinating is how hard those differences are to discover. We all say, “Imagine an apple,” and assume that everybody else is having something like our experience. But the same words may describe quite different experiences. I’d be cautious about going from that difference in experience to a claim that a whole computational process is broken.

r001.rationale: The response discusses top-down processing and representations but does not mention visual-cortex activation or describe it as a side effect.

r002.rationale: It suggests some representations may remain without conscious pictures, but does not clearly state that the capacity to generate visual representations remains intact.
